settingsPermissions.heading: Permissions
settingsPermissions.subtitle: Rules decide which tool calls run without asking, and which are blocked outright. A deny rule beats execute mode and auto-approve — but it only ever matches one literal command or path, and it cannot see inside a compound command. Review them here, revoke any of them, and pick up suggestions drawn from your history.
settingsPermissions.unavailable: Only available in the installed app — this page needs the engine.
settingsPermissions.inactiveHint: This entry is malformed, so it has no effect. Delete it to tidy up.
settingsPermissions.deleteBody.allow: Next time a call matches {rule}, AWOG will ask again.
settingsPermissions.deleteBody.deny: This one is a guardrail. Remove it and calls matching {rule} are no longer blocked — they go back to being asked about, and can be let through.
settingsPermissions.scope.session: Session {name} — forgotten when the engine stops
settingsPermissions.corrupt.title: Broken rule file
settingsPermissions.corrupt.body: Cannot read {file} ({reason}). Every rule in it — deny rules included — is currently inactive. Fix the file by hand, then reload.
settingsPermissions.list.heading: Saved rules
settingsPermissions.list.empty: No rules yet. Each “Always allow” you press in a session adds one here.
settingsPermissions.suggest.heading: Suggestions from history
settingsPermissions.suggest.desc: Being asked about the same command over and over is what makes people click through. Scan recent sessions for commands that ran many times and no rule covers yet.
settingsPermissions.suggest.truncated: Scan limit reached — this is not the whole history.
settingsPermissions.suggest.safety: Only single commands that finished repeatedly and no rule covers are suggested. Compound commands, privilege escalation (sudo…) and commands containing a wildcard are never suggested. Nothing becomes a rule on its own — you have to press.
settingsPermissions.deny.heading: Block a tool
settingsPermissions.deny.desc: A deny rule beats every relaxation — execute mode, auto-approve, and a permission you just granted. Write the tool name to turn it off completely (e.g. Artifact), or narrow it with a pattern (e.g. Bash(rm *)).
